title: Incident Surge Stabilizer — Lite Steps (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, pragmatic runbook for rapid triage during short, high-impact infrastructure surges that affect GPU-backed inference capacity. It is intentionally lightweight so first responders can act within the first 10–60 minutes to stabilize traffic, recover capacity, and prevent downstream timeouts.

Scope and when to use this doc:
- Use for short-duration incidents causing >20% loss of inference capacity in a single region or measurable SLO degradation (p99 latency spike or increased 5xxs).
- Not intended for planned maintenance, long-term capacity planning, or hardware RMA workflows. Those have separate procedures.

Roles and responsibilities:
- Oncall (primary): ownership of initial triage, customer communication, and executing lightweight remediations.
- Infra lead (backup): coordinates longer fixes (node replacement, driver rollbacks), approves capacity adds.
- Cloud/HW tech: authorizes/executes physical GPU swaps or provider-level reboots if needed.
- Engineering incident commander (IC): for incidents that escalate beyond 60 minutes or cross regions.

Quick decision matrix (high level):
- Pattern A: Single node failure but remaining capacity healthy -> cordon + drain + backfill temp node.
- Pattern B: Multiple nodes with driver/kernel faults -> isolate by taint + revert recent infra change -> scale down susceptible pools.
- Pattern C: Throttled throughput with kernel OOMs or PCIe errors -> evict noisy pods, enable degraded routing to CPU-backed lightweight models.

First 10 minutes — immediate actions (do these in parallel where safe):
1) Confirm incident: check alerts (pager duty, datadog), console error rates, and host telemetry. Capture top-3 failing stacks.
2) Put an incident banner in the #sre channel and short triage note: region, observed impact, initial hypothesis, primary oncall.
3) Reduce incoming pressure: temporarily enable rate-limiting or routing to fallback models (see routing playbook), if available.
4) Identify suspect nodes: kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep -E "gpu|accelerator" and map to cloud instance ids.
5) Set a temp capacity floor: if autoscaler is aggressive, pause scale-in policies to avoid compounding losses.

Commands cheatlist (kubectl + provider):
- List nodes: kubectl get nodes -o wide --show-labels
- Check pods on node: kubectl get pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=<NODE> -o wide
- Cordon node: kubectl cordon <NODE>
- Drain node (conservative): kubectl drain <NODE> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector="app!=critical-sidecar" --grace-period=120
- Add taint for isolation: kubectl taint nodes <NODE> critical=isolated:NoSchedule --overwrite
- Provider soft reboot: gcloud compute instances reset <INSTANCE> (or provider-equivalent)
- Warm node registration: ssh into node, verify nvidia-smi, check driver versions, run smoke inference test script.

Triage heuristics for GPU vs driver vs infra network faults:
- GPU hardware fault: PCIe errors, ECC correctable/unrecoverable logs, repeated nvidia-smi failures.
- Driver/kernel fault: segfaults in nvidia modules, kernel oops referencing nv or nouveau, driver upgrades in last 24h.
post_content:
(continued)
- Container runtime: dockerd/containerd crash loops, plugin errors. Check kubelet logs: journalctl -u kubelet -n 200

Safe node isolation pattern (recommended order):
1) kubectl cordon <NODE> to stop new allocations.
2) kubectl taint nodes <NODE> critical=isolated:NoSchedule to ensure no new pods (redundant but explicit).
3) Evict non-critical pods with kubectl delete pod --namespace=<NS> <POD> --grace-period=30 if drain stalls.
4) If pods fail to terminate, escalate to infra lead for node reboot or forceful eviction.

Lightweight capacity onramp (fast path):
- Purpose: quickly restore serving capacity while avoiding long RMA or hardware swap in the critical window.
Steps:
1) Query warm pool: check preprovisioned warm nodes (internal tag: warm-gpu-pool). If available, trigger scale-up by toggling tag or API: ops-cli provision warm-node --region <R>.
2) If warm pool empty, spin up smallest compatible instance type with existing AMI (use gpu-min-ami-2026-01) to bring topology online faster. Use provider autoscale template for minimal bootstrapping.
3) After node boots, run warm-registration script: /opt/redwood/bin/node-warm-register.sh --smoke-test=all. Wait for healthcheck to pass.
4) Remove any autoscaler pause and allow k8s to schedule pods to the new node. Monitor p99 latency and error rate.

When to do a physical GPU replacement vs soft-reboot/cold-swap:
- Do physical replacement if (a) ECC unrecoverable hardware errors, (b) vendor RMA requires swap, (c) repeated device detach logs after soft reboots.
- Prefer soft-reboot -> driver rollback -> reimage if logs point to driver/kernel regressions. Physical swap is slow and reserved for confirmed HW faults.

Rollback and fallback policies (prevent bad rollouts):
- If an infra change (driver/AMI) was deployed within last 24h and we see correlated failures, trigger immediate rollback to previous AMI and stop new cluster rollouts.
- Apply traffic-splitting: divert 30–50% to stable region or cheaper CPU fallback until p99 stabilizes.

Observability and checkpoints to collect (evidence collection):
- Host logs: dmesg, journalctl -u kubelet -n 500, /var/log/nvidia-installer.log, /var/log/cloud-init-output.log
- GPU telemetry: nvidia-smi -q -x, vendor tool output, GPU ECC/thermal stats
- K8s events: kubectl get events --all-namespaces --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
- Application traces: trace ids of failing requests, top stacks (sampling).
- Save ticket: attach logs to JIRA-PI-4821 and snapshot VM console output.

Cooldown and next steps after stabilization (first 60–240 minutes):
- Confirm traffic restored and p99 within acceptable SLO band for 30 minutes.
- If hardware RMA needed, schedule physical replacement in maintenance window; prepare capacity padding for the RMA.
- If a software regression implicated, create rollback PR and schedule controlled rollout with canary.
- Start post-incident timeline notes in the incident doc and assign owners for root cause analysis.

Post-incident: minimal postmortem checklist (owner: IC)
- TL;DR and incident timeline with decisions and timestamps.
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence.
- What worked/what didn't: actions that reduced blast radius and actions that caused noise.
- Follow-ups: driver pinning, improve warm pool sizing, update autoscaler thresholds.
- Action owners and due dates.

Helpful quick-snippets (copy-ready):
- cordon + drain conservative:
  kubectl cordon NODE-1 && kubectl drain NODE-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
- list GPU errors on host:
  sudo dmesg | grep -i -E "nv|nvidia|gpu|ecc|pci" | tail -n 200
- smoke inference test (example):
  curl -X POST https://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"smoke test"}' --insecure -H 'Authorization: Bearer $LOCAL_TOKEN'

Open questions / TODOs for this doc:
- Define exact SLO thresholds that should auto-trigger the lightweight onramp (ops: Lina).
- Add provider-agnostic scripts for warm provisioning (ops: Owen).
- Include a decision tree graphic for triage (design: Samir).

Related docs and further reading:
- See linked artifacts at top. Also: infra/driver-compat-matrix (internal Confluence), k8s-pod-eviction-policies (internal page).

Notes to future oncall: this is intentionally terse. If you have more than 60 minutes of active troubleshooting, escalate to IC and switch to the full incident runbook. Keep chronological notes in the incident timeline and err on the side of reducing customer traffic rather than high-risk physical interventions.

End of lightweight stabilizer doc.
